items.title: Bioenergetics and ATP: the energy currency of cells

source_refs.note: Chapter opening and the ATP section, printed pages 140-141: bioenergetics, the structure of ATP, the high-energy bonds and the ATP-ADP cycle. The topic is unnumbered in print.

blocks.text: Every living organism, from the smallest bacterium to the largest whale, is driven by energy. This energy fuels growth, reproduction and daily survival, making it a fundamental aspect of life. Where does this energy come from, and how is it harnessed and used by cells to perform the countless activities essential for life? The answer lies in bioenergetics.

blocks.title: Bioenergetics
blocks.text: Bioenergetics is the study of how energy flows through living systems. It explores the processes through which cells store and expend energy. Photosynthesis and respiration illustrate its principles: photosynthesis is an energy-capturing process and respiration an energy-releasing one.

blocks.title: Where almost all energy comes from
blocks.text: Nearly all the energy used by living organisms on Earth comes from photosynthesis. Plants, algae and certain bacteria capture sunlight and convert it into chemical energy, forming the base of the food chain.
ATP: the energy currency of cells

Cells use a special energy currency for their reactions: a nucleotide called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). When cells store energy they make ATP; when they need energy they break ATP. A molecule of ATP has three subunits: adenine (a nitrogen-containing base), ribose (a five-carbon sugar) and three phosphate groups.

blocks.title: Discovery
blocks.text: ATP was discovered in 1929 by Karl Lohmann. In 1941 the Nobel prize winner Fritz Lipmann proposed that ATP is the main energy-transfer molecule in the cell.

The covalent bonds between two phosphates are high-energy bonds. When one of these bonds is broken, inorganic phosphate (Pi) separates and energy is released: the breaking of one phosphate bond releases about 7.3 kcal (7,300 calories) per mole of ATP. In common energy reactions only the outer P-P high-energy bond breaks; ATP becomes ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and one Pi is released. In some cases ADP is further broken down to AMP (adenosine monophosphate) and Pi, again releasing 7.3 kcal per mole.

blocks.alt: Left: the ATP molecule as adenine, a ribose pentagon and three phosphate circles, with red curved high-energy bonds between the phosphates. Right: a cycle of two arrows between ATP at the top and ADP plus Pi at the bottom, the downward arrow labelled breakdown with water and energy released, the upward arrow labelled formation with energy from the oxidation of food.
blocks.caption: The structure of ATP and the ATP-ADP cycle (original diagram after Figures 5.1 and 5.2 of the chapter).
blocks.long_description: ATP is adenine, ribose and three phosphates; the bonds between the phosphates are high-energy bonds. Breaking the outer bond with water gives ADP, inorganic phosphate and about 7.3 kcal per mole; ADP can lose another phosphate to become AMP. Cells remake ATP by joining ADP and Pi with energy from the oxidation of food, so ATP is made during energy-releasing processes and broken during energy-consuming ones, carrying energy between metabolic reactions.

blocks.caption: The two breakdown reactions
rows: ATP + H2O gives ADP + Pi + energy
ADP + H2O gives AMP + Pi + energy

blocks.text: Cells get energy from the oxidation of food. They store this energy by combining ADP with Pi to form ATP. So ATP is made during energy-releasing processes and broken down during energy-consuming processes; in this way ATP transfers energy between metabolic reactions.

blocks.prompt: Why is ATP called a currency rather than a store of energy?
blocks.explanation: Like money, ATP is not kept for long but passed from one process to another: energy-releasing reactions such as the oxidation of food pay energy in by joining ADP and Pi, and energy-consuming reactions spend it by breaking the high-energy phosphate bond. It transfers energy rather than storing it.

items: Bioenergetics studies the flow of energy through living systems; photosynthesis captures energy and respiration releases it. Nearly all energy for life comes from photosynthesis.
ATP (Lohmann 1929; Lipmann 1941) is adenine + ribose + three phosphates with high-energy P-P bonds. ATP + H2O gives ADP + Pi + 7.3 kcal per mole; ADP can go on to AMP.
ATP is made when food is oxidised (ADP + Pi) and broken when energy is needed: the cell's energy currency.
